newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan defends bid to name U.S. centre for Chiang.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan defends bid to name U.S. centre for Chiang.

text.p: A Taiwan-funded foundation defended on Wednesday its push to name a planned U.S. research centre after late President Chiang Ching-kuo, blaming a brewing controversy on "anti-Asia" sentiment in America.
The Chiang Ching-kuo Foundation said it would insist the centre be named after Chiang if the University of California at Berkeley accepts its US$3 million endowment.

Some U.C. Berkeley officials object to the centre bearing the name of Chiang -- who ran Taiwan's secret police under martial law but later cultivated the seeds of democracy and broke the political back of his own "Chiang dynasty".
"If we provide the funding for the centre, then we feel we have every right to have the centre named after our foundation," foundation vice president James Chiang said by telephone.

California's San Jose Mercury News said on Monday that some Berkeley professors feared the name would compromise the centre's objectivity and honour a man who for most of his 1978-88 presidency was an uncompromising dictator.

"It is ludicrous to say that just because the centre is named after Chiang Ching-kuo, we are trying to politically influence its research," said Chiang, who is unrelated to the once-powerful Chiang family.
Chiang denied threatening to withdraw a recent US$15 million gift made to Berkeley by unidentified Taiwan alumni unless the prestigious school agreed to open a Chiang centre.
"Our foundation did not make the US$15 million donation so that donation is good regardless of what happens to the US$3 million centre," he said.

The centre, which would fund Chinese history research, has political overtones because Washington recognises only the Chinese communist government in Beijing, Taiwan's arch rival since a civil war split them in 1949.
Chiang Ching-kuo's father, Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, retreated to Taiwan with his Nationalist government after its defeat by the communists.
His family ruled Taiwan with an iron fist until the younger Chiang began democratic reforms before he died in 1988.
Taiwan's Republic of China government, recognised by only 30 states, acknowledges using state and Nationalist Party money in a drive to break free from its Beijing-imposed isolation.
Although the Chiang Foundation got half of its T$2.6 billion endowment from the state, James Chiang insisted it had no political motives and served purely academic goals.
"We are ready to provide a list of all past recipients of our scholarships. Berkeley can ask any one of them whether we have ever tried to influence their research," Chiang said.

He said the issue has been overblown amid controversy over suspected illegal contributions from Asian donors -- including Taiwan's Nationalist Party -- to both major U.S. political parties and President Bill Clinton's re-election campaign.
"There's definitely an anti-Asia sentiment sweeping the U.S. right now. We just got hit at a bad time," Chiang said.
Chiang said one Berkeley professor quoted by the Mercury News as speaking out against the proposed centre, Elizabeth Perry, was herself a recipient of a Chiang foundation grant.
"Ask Professor Perry whether we have ever interfered with her work," Chiang said.
Perry was quoted by the paper as saying: "It would be a bad precedent for an American university to take on the name of Chiang Ching-kuo or take on programmes with his name on them."
The foundation grants about US$6 million a year in academic scholarships all over the world, about half to U.S. scholars.
The foundation also has approached the University of Chicago and Columbia University about housing the Chiang centre.
